The Great Wall's secret glue? Sticky rice. 🍚 Watch the Ming-era wall go up in 25 seconds. ⏱️

The Ming dynasty built the wall you picture today between the 14th and 17th centuries, following the ridgelines over hill after hill: a stone foundation, an earth-and-rubble core, a skin of fired bricks, battlements and watchtowers.

The twist: sections were bonded with lime mortar mixed with sticky-rice soup. The starch in the rice (amylopectin) makes the mortar tougher and far more water-resistant, which is part of why it's still standing 400+ years later.

Would you eat the rice or build with it? 👇

yt_description:
The recognizable Ming sections of the Great Wall were built between the 14th and 17th centuries. Parts were bonded with slaked-lime mortar mixed with sticky-rice soup; amylopectin from the rice refines the mortar's pore structure, giving high fracture toughness and low water permeability. Sticky-rice mortar has been used in China for at least 1,500 years.

Sources: https://ceramics.org/ceramic-tech-today/ming-dynasty-sticky-rice-mortar/ · https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/67539/15-colossal-facts-about-great-wall-china
